nodes.title: Record board: three games
nodes.gist: The project plays three games: the height game (largest g, N unbounded), the threshold game T(Q) (smallest N with g above Q) and the budget game R(X) (largest g with N below X). Your question is the budget game.
nodes.detail: Board at the research branch's last update (2026-11-21): height 10,000,141 at a 61,329-digit N; threshold, a 150-digit N with g = 104,527; budget 119,419. The GPU fleet raised the budget record to 158,209 on 2026-11-23 and to 160,357 on 2026-11-24. Exhaustive search shows g(N) ≤ 9,781 for every even N up to 4×10^18, so every constructive record is far beyond it. A record must say which bound it meets: R(10^199) and R(10^200) are different games. The research branch named 158,209 only after review (commit 02564fb); the fleet's hits file still showed 157,837 then. The fleet's hits file was last updated on 23 Nov 02:10 UTC; near-miss records are in each record's own folder.

note.text: Everything on this map is in service of one number: the largest g(N) for N below 10^200.

nodes.title: The 200-digit fleet campaign (budget game)
nodes.gist: GPUs scan arithmetic progressions N₀ + t·M built on a cover of 88–89 odd primes. The budget record rose 125,269 → 133,981 → 146,191 → 157,837 → 158,209 → 160,357 between 2026-11-22 and 2026-11-24 (the 119,419 before them was a July CPU record).
nodes.detail: At 02:40 UTC on 2026-11-23 about 10 fleet-days of compute were left, at 29 million effective full-weight members per second; the planning model now uses 8.9 days from 24 Nov 04:05 UTC at 52 million (model units), and the fleet shrank on 24 Nov (see ‘The fleet now’). The fleet reports near-misses: the first probable-prime row of a tested member is g(N), so designs aimed at 170,000 produced the 158,209 and 160,357 records. The records live on the fleet's branch; the Lean library re-certifies them. The covers now include the 491 set (first 88 odd primes and 491) and the first-88 set on the smaller cards.

note.text: This is the engine that produced the record. The Lean file only certifies its output.

nodes.title: Height game: 1.2 million to 10 million, no ECPP
nodes.gist: Letting the Chinese remainder theorem make N − g carry its own one-exponentiation primality proof, together with complete covers, took the height record from 1,157,341 to 10,000,141 in two days.
nodes.detail: Records: 1,200,109 (11,263 digits, certified twice for two different N), 2,000,269 (15,595 digits), 5,000,251 (33,938 digits) and 10,000,141 (61,329 digits, a 9,095-class cover, about two hours on a Colab A100). The next rung, g above 16,045,848, would beat the largest known prime gap; it is costed at about 13 days on 4 cores and was not done.

note.text: A different game from yours (N unbounded), but it shows what removing the certification wall bought.

nodes.title: The 2,692-digit megagap: g = 1,134,871
nodes.gist: A 2,692-digit N whose least Goldbach summand 1,134,871 exceeds the largest certified prime gap (1,113,106), while the prime gap around N is only 8,970.
nodes.detail: Of the 88,239 primes below g, one is excluded by parity, 85,476 by a cover divisor, 895 by trial division and 1,867 by failed Fermat tests; N − g has a 253-step ECPP certificate. Found on 2026-07-21 with a search exponent of 6.56.

note.text: Shows a Goldbach desert need not be a prime gap: it only has to make the sparse set N − q composite.

nodes.title: Threshold game: from 186 down to 150 digits, and the low end
nodes.gist: The smallest known N with g above 100,000 fell from 186 digits to 179 to 150 (g = 104,527, found by a GPU engine). At the low end, a 23-digit N (3.06×10^22) has g above 10,000, found by the fscan scanner.
nodes.detail: The 150-digit jump came from throughput, not new mathematics: the CUDA engine was about 430 times the 4-core pipeline, and ln 430 = 6.1 nats matches the gap in the cost exponent. Five 23-digit numbers with g above 10,000 appeared where 0.78 were expected, an unexplained 0.13% event. The threshold game at g ≥ 10^6 has started as a cover only (629 moduli, 3,028 rows left): nothing found or certified.

nodes.title: Selective testing: test only the emptiest members (the 3% rule)
nodes.gist: After sieving, count the rows each candidate still has alive and run the expensive Fermat tests only on the few percent with the fewest. This gives roughly a 3× net speed-up.
nodes.detail: A candidate with k rows left succeeds with probability about (1 − p)^k, so a small fraction holds a large share of the successes: the fleet's 3% rule holds 15.6%, worth 2.0 nats. Sieving deeper (to 10^8 on the newest cards) adds about 28% more expected successes per second. Since 23 Nov the 3% rule holds only on the L4s and the T4: the RTX cards keep the emptiest 1.5% (keep fraction 0.985, design hits a second ×1.10 over 0.97), and the L4 test at 0.985 failed (×0.9865). The sieve depth was re-optimised jointly with the keep fraction for today's engine: 10^8 stays (the best alternative is +1.2% at keep fraction 0.99; deeper sieves lose).

note.text: The cheapest measured speed-up in the programme, and a constant factor: it does not change the exponent.

nodes.title: GPU Fermat engines
nodes.gist: CUDA code sieves a block of candidates and runs a Montgomery base-2 Fermat test on each surviving row, around 20 million tests per second on a modern card. A separate engine screens the 60,000-digit candidates of the height game.
nodes.detail: Validated bit for bit against Python and gmpy2; every GPU hit is re-proved on a CPU, so a GPU error can waste time but not forge a record. Throughput history: 2.5M tests per second on a T4, 8.5M on an A100, 22.9M on an RTX PRO 6000 with 28-bit limbs. Since 23 Nov: 24.6M tests a second with the 29-bit kernel (+5.7% on the 23 Nov baseline) and 23.4M for the best 28-bit step; a window's sieve phase fell from 83.7 to 44.4 ms and an RTX batch from 0.945 to about 0.73 s (see ‘The GPU sieve chain’); a new IFMA CPU test for 300 to 400 digits is 8 to 12 times gmpy2.

note.text: The Lean library proves three of these kernels compute exactly the Fermat test.

nodes.title: fscan and tscan: CPU scanners for the low end
nodes.gist: tscan sieves blocks of candidates and tests those with few rows left. fscan scores 64 candidates per vector instruction and Fermat-tests the best 0.3%, 24 at a time (AVX-512), about 4.5 times tscan per core-second.
nodes.detail: The gain is a constant factor. Searching over more than 13 fixed primes, or sharing the sieve between neighbouring numbers, did not help. The 52-, 26- and 30-bit kernels and the residue step are the ones Lean proves correct.

note.text: Used for the threshold game at 20–60 digits; not part of the 200-digit record apart from the 'score first' idea.

nodes.title: Cover design: greedy, annealing, parallel tempering
nodes.gist: Choosing a residue class for each modulus is a set-cover-like design problem. For 200 digits, a parallel-tempering sampler on the 89 odd primes 3..463 finds covers leaving 1,248 rows at Q = 170,000 and 1,609 rows at the 10% target 213,070.
nodes.detail: Greedy plus annealing gives 867 rows at Q = 122,000 (plain greedy 912); tempering finds 851, and the Lean session's independent sampler 850. One more modulus buys about 14 rows for 5.3 digits of modulus; one extra row costs 2.4% of success probability per member. Until 24 Nov there was no closed formula for the optimum and no proof of a floor; now there is a derived predictor (1,221 rows at 170,000, 1,584 at 213,070, within 2% of the best found), measured floors (1,214; 1,554 to 1,596), a certified floor of 777 rows (exhaustive) and a linear-programme floor of 1,170 for fixed small classes. The 89-prime optimum 1,248 is confirmed three ways (186 covers at 1,248); with 491 as the 89th prime the best is 1,245. Evolved (AlphaEvolve) cover optimisers were not competitive. A greedy-plus-descent code (archipelago session) leaves 1,309 rows at the campaign's point against 1,248 tempered; tempering at 30 to 302 moduli reaches 0.78 to 0.88 · x ln² x.

note.text: Going from 88 to 89 moduli gave 1.27 times the success rate: one of the few places where mathematics, not compute, moved the record.

nodes.title: The Lean session's cover experiments: 850 rows at Q = 122,000
nodes.gist: The Lean session wrote its own replica-exchange sampler over residue vectors and counted vectors by rows left. At Q = 122,000 on the campaign's 88 moduli it found a cover leaving 850 rows (the campaign's greedy cover: 867), plus bulk lists of near-best vectors for the fleet.
nodes.detail: Random vectors leave 1,376.9 rows on average (standard deviation 20.2); the greedy cover is 25 deviations below. There are e^436 vectors in all, e^43 with at most 867 rows, and the count reaches one near 850. The best cover costs about 0.21 nats per 1,000 in Q. Beyond the design target a further prime stays alive with probability 0.12, so surviving past the design value by luck is nearly as cheap as designing for it. Adding 443, 449 and 457 would give 831 rows but leave only about 60 members per vector.

note.text: Its agreement with the research session's own sampler (851) is the evidence that the plateau near 850 is the optimum for 88 moduli.

nodes.title: Complete covers: 15,907 on 89 primes, 16,747 on 92
nodes.gist: Cover every prime below Q with no leftover row, so no luck is needed. On the 89 odd primes up to 463 the best found reaches 15,907 (1,853 primes below it); on 91, 92 and 93 primes, 16,381, 16,747 and 16,981 (all certified in Lean).
nodes.detail: At 15,950 and 16,000 the best covers on 89 primes leave one row, so complete covers on the 89 primes end near 16,000 (by a measured count of covers), and 15,907 ≤ D(89) < 35,000 is proved by exhaustive search. From 92 primes on a cover below 10^200 exists only for a fraction of the residue choices, so the research session finds one by enumeration, as the Chinese-remainder line's sharpness predicts. A 94th prime (499) does not pay; a local search around the cover finds nothing; complete covers continue on larger sets to 41,659 (167 moduli, Lean-checked), 70,111 (238) and 98,731 (302).

note.text: 0.7% of the ceiling, against 7.5% found by search: what can be constructed is far behind what search finds.

nodes.title: Verification: three independent legs
nodes.gist: Every height record passes three separately written checkers (a standard-library Python verifier, a second one that rebuilds N by product-tree CRT, and PARI's own N − 1 certificate plus a brute-force scan). A mutation test rejects all 11 corrupted copies.
nodes.detail: Older records carry a PARI elliptic-curve certificate re-checked by an independent checker plus a witness for every prime below g. A fail-open flaw was found on 2026-11-22 (gp carried on after an error); no committed log is affected and the packaging script now stops on error.

note.text: No record rests on the scanner that found it. The Lean library adds a machine-checked fourth leg for the budget-game records.

nodes.title: Cost model: E = |U| · boost / ln N
nodes.gist: A candidate in a progression succeeds when every one of the |U| rows the cover misses is composite. Each is prime with probability about boost/ln N, so about e^E candidates are needed per success, with E = |U|·boost/ln N and boost = 2·∏ r/(r − 1).
nodes.detail: Checked against measurements to about 0.1 nats: toy 62 digits 13.52 predicted against 13.57 measured, the 197-digit record 18.2 against 18.2, the 2,692-digit record 6.6 against 6.56. Campaign 3's logged value ran 0.2–0.4 nats above theory, which its log flagged as ‘watching’. The model rests on independence of the rows (hypothesis H1), which is an assumption, not a theorem. The model counts rows below the design level Q only. The final record also depends on the uncovered primes above Q: a success must survive each with probability 1 − p, confirmed at Q = 60,000 (1,184 against 1,186 successes, landing shifted ×1.23); see ‘Rows above the design level’.

note.text: Every price in the programme comes from this one formula. Its unit is the nat: a factor of e in the number of candidates.

nodes.title: Heuristic ceiling: about 2.13 million at 200 digits
nodes.gist: The Hardy–Littlewood prime-tuple heuristic, with no fitted constant, predicts the largest g(N) to expect below N: 9,570 at 19 digits, 465,350 at 100 digits, 2,130,704 at 200 digits.
nodes.detail: Checked on 600 million random even N near 10^18, agreeing within 0.5%. The campaign's yardsticks come from it: 7.41% is 157,837, and the 10% target is 213,070. An earlier fitted constant (C ≈ 1.4) was replaced by the computed one, which lowered every closeness figure; the ratio to ln²N · ln ln N grows from 1.40 to 1.64. The window records near 10^12, 10^15 and 10^18 match it as well (see 'Tested: the records of each window'). Lean's independent closed formula (one constant fitted on the scan of every even N up to 10^12) puts the expected maximum below 10^200 at 2,133,689, 0.14% above; the ceiling is known to about 0.4%.

note.text: The 10% target is 10% of a model, not of a theorem. The standing record 160,357 is 7.53% of it.

nodes.title: Price list: what raising the target costs
nodes.gist: At 200 digits one expected success costs 0.8 card-days (0.2 fleet-days) at a design target of 150,000, 7.7 card-days at 160,000, 436 at 180,000, 26,627 at 200,000, and 400,099 card-days (about 1,100 card-years) at 213,070.
nodes.detail: A success lands about 4,100 above the design target, and every +10,000 in g costs a factor of 8 to 9. For a fixed fraction of the ceiling the exponent grows with the number of digits: 20% needs E near 80. The ‘about 4,100’ depends on the cover's uncovered primes above the design level: at Q = 60,000 the mean landing was 3,766 above for family B against 3,071 for A (41 against 55 uncovered primes in the next 4,000). The fleet-days column assumes 1,262 rows on 88 moduli and an older engine; the fleet's own logs give 0.29 design hits a day at 7 GPUs, 3.7 times faster than priced.

nodes.title: What the remaining budget buys
nodes.gist: The planning model now expects a final record of about 175,000–176,000 (8.2% of the ceiling), with a chance of the 10% target below 0.01%; the earlier figure was 169,000–172,500 from a record of 157,837 with about 10 fleet-days left. Aiming straight at 213,070 would need about 50,749 fleet-days, some 5,600 times the remaining budget.
nodes.detail: The best design for a limited budget aims below the target: a cover built for 172,500 beats one built for 213,070 by eight points. A week of the fleet is worth about 167,000, a month 174,000, a year 186,000 (model extrapolations). The newer figure comes from a faster measured rate (52 million effective members per second from 24 Nov 04:05 UTC) and the family-B designs (+1,000); it does not include the fleet's shrinking on 24 Nov. note.text: The honest answer to ‘can we reach 10%’: not by search alone with the compute in hand. The standing record 160,357 sits below the expected final value, so more near-misses are likely.

nodes.title: Two budgets: nats of modulus and nats of work
nodes.gist: A prime used to build N costs ln r of the 460.5 nats available below 10^200, whether it fixes one class or many. Information beyond that can only be collected by enumerating candidates and counting rows: one nat of work per nat of information.
nodes.detail: The campaign's allocation of moduli is optimal to about 0.2 nats. Allowing k classes instead of one gains only 1–2.8 nats at 100–150 digits, and the classic cover is the unique design that is free to enumerate. An oracle ignoring the size limit would reach E = 25.75 with 200 moduli, against 39.2 for the 88 in use.

note.text: Sizes the prize beyond the modulus budget at about 10 nats. That is where the sublinear search question comes from.

nodes.title: H1: the leftover rows are independent
nodes.gist: Given all the divisibility information, the primality of distinct leftover rows is independent, with Mertens-adjusted probabilities (a Hardy–Littlewood style local model).
nodes.detail: Not implied by GRH: it is a k-tuple statement. Support: the cost model matches measurements to about 0.1 nats over 1.2×10^9 candidates. But campaign 3 ran 0.2–0.4 nats above theory, and a first-moment match does not obviously constrain the joint probability that all rows are composite. Since this snapshot Lean proves that, inside the residue model and for primes above Q, independence is a safe upper bound; the residue model itself and the rows below Q stay heuristic. Since then, two kinds of support: the thinning law (Lean) makes independence an upper bound for the moduli above Q, and an exhaustive test on 60 million numbers near 10^12 to 10^18 finds the chance that every row is composite within about 1% of the model, conditionally on the sieve, for pairs of neighbours too, and up to each window's record. A direct test at Q = 60,000 (1,184 against 1,186 successes) agrees with (1 − p)^rows, and a closed formula with one fitted constant for the dependence between the rows of one N reproduces the prize counts to within 0.1 nats.

note.text: Every cost forecast and the closure theorem assume it.

nodes.title: H2: no compositeness test cheaper than one exponentiation
nodes.gist: Does a randomized algorithm exist that decides compositeness of a random rough 660-bit number in time below one modular exponentiation? The closure theorem assumes not.
nodes.detail: No lower bound is known in any realistic model. A detector with cost c and recall r would speed up the Fermat-first pipeline by 1/(c + (1 − r)): c = 0.1 and r = 0.9 would give 5×. More than 95% of engine time is base-2 Fermat tests, about 17 per candidate.

note.text: The one identified escape from the cost floor of the search. The sublinear programme's rung 5 is its integer counterpart.

nodes.title: Divisor-Paradigm Closure Theorem
nodes.gist: No construction whose compositeness certificates are planted divisor identities (congruences, polynomial values, exponential families, multivariate forms, norm forms, cyclotomic values, compositions) beats the covering frontier, assuming H1 and H2.
nodes.detail: A draft-rigour theorem on a grammar of seven schema families the authors chose. Zero passes among 13,661 hand-enumerated instances and 41 machine-evolved candidates; the best was 53 times too expensive. Mechanisms outside the grammar are not excluded. The thesis itself says ‘at the level of rigour of a well-supported research programme’.

note.text: Why the programme concludes that the only levers left are the rounding gap (0–2.6 nats of mathematics) and compute.

nodes.title: Lemma: a shared divisor divides q₁ − q₂
nodes.gist: If d divides both N − q₁ and N − q₂ for two primes below Q, then d divides q₁ − q₂, so d is itself below Q.
nodes.detail: All dependence between rows therefore runs through primes below Q, which the cover fixes and the sieve harvests. This is a deterministic fact (Proposition 2a); the conditional half (2b) needs H1.

note.text: Proved on paper by the research session and, with the same content, in Lean as lt_of_dvd_two_rows. Neither document cites the other.

nodes.title: Planted certificates cost at least covering's marginal price
nodes.gist: Whatever the family, certifying one more row N − q composite costs at least what a covering congruence would. Congruence classes cost ln d, polynomial identities certify at most √Q rows, exponential families run out of supply, multivariate forms cluster only up to 13 rows.
nodes.detail: Closure family by family: polynomial values of degree 2 or more, at most 349 rows at Q = 122,000; exponential families, 1,048 rows would cost 1,151 nats against a budget of 460; multivariate forms with fewer variables than degree, at most 13 rows against about 18,000 needed; window-dense families, isolation and orbit arguments; compositions, empty at 10^200. Several are first-moment arguments at draft rigour.

note.text: The quantitative core of why the ‘third mechanism’ does not exist inside the grammar.

nodes.title: Falsification engine: 13,661 instances, zero passes
nodes.gist: An engine that scores any proposed certificate scheme against covering's price was calibrated on hand numbers, swept over 13,661 schema instances, then attacked by an evolutionary search driven by a language model. No scheme passed.
nodes.detail: The first evolved candidates exploited a hole in the referee: offsets were billed only against the 867 leftover primes, so 10,416 offsets cost 22,900 nats against a budget of 460, a 50-fold overdraft. After the fix the best fitness is 53 times too expensive. The lesson recorded: adversarial search is most useful as referee hardening.

note.text: Shows the closure benchmark was hardened by an adversary before it was trusted.

nodes.title: Five probes of non-covering mechanisms all end
nodes.gist: Prime-power moduli kill nothing new. Polynomial identities N = mᵏ − c kill at most O(√Q) rows. Exponent families and norm forms reduce to covering. Any leftover bias in the leftover rows is worth at most 0.1 nats.
nodes.detail: Predeclared gates; all five terminated. The research states three conditions any real mechanism must meet: certify far more than √Q rows, cost o(ln r) design entropy per row, and stay invisible in bulk statistics. Covering manages about 4,400 offsets per nat at r = 3, falling to 0.4 at r ≈ 1,200.

note.text: Lean proves the exact statements behind probes P1 and P2 (prime moduli suffice; the value-set ceiling).

nodes.title: Door 1: the rounding gap
nodes.gist: The set-cover LP says the cover is 100% fractionally feasible, so it certifies nothing: the whole cost exponent is an integrality gap. At Q = 122,000 a random assignment leaves about 1,377 primes uncovered, greedy 867, and an annealed first-moment threshold suggests 758.
nodes.detail: In July, forty-one exact windows, belief-propagation decimation (874) and an exact half-cover block found nothing below 867, so 867 was judged at or near the optimum and the prize shrank from about 2.6 nats to 0–2.6. Later, parallel tempering found 850–851 rows at the same Q on the same moduli (0.4 nats better), and its density of states reaches one vector near 850: part of the prize has been collected and the rest looks small. All of this is evidence, not a global certificate. Since 24 Nov door 1 is measured: at Q = 170,000 the best cover (1,248 rows) is 34 rows (0.83 nat, a factor of at most 2.3) above the measured floor 1,214, and at 213,070 the best (1,609) is within 1.3 nats of the floors 1,554 to 1,596. The ‘annealed first-moment threshold’ is explained: the first-moment count is off by 1.35·ln Q/ln x in the loss (it predicts about 790 rows at 170,000; 1,248 were found). The only theorem is the exhaustive floor of 777 rows.

note.text: The place where mathematics bought nats: about 0.4 of them so far. Each nat is a factor of about 2.7 in compute.

nodes.title: Three doors: mathematics, compute, paradigm
nodes.gist: Every route to a higher record passes through one of three doors: the rounding gap (mathematics), the ticket rate (compute), or a new compositeness mechanism (the paradigm). Door 3 is closed on the grammar, Door 1 is measured to be nearly exhausted (a floor under every cover, within 0.8 nat of the best), Door 2 is the reliable one.
nodes.detail: Divisor information is fully harvested by the sieve; correlation between rows implies a common divisor; certificates are either planted (paying ln r per row) or extracted (factoring-equivalent). Records are logarithmic in compute: each factor of 10 buys 2.3 nats. The measurement is empirical; the only theorem, the exhaustive floor of 777 rows against the best cover's 1,248, is far from closing the door.

note.text: The programme-level plan: compute, plus a small chance from mathematics.

nodes.title: Operation Staircase: a compute ladder to 200,000
nodes.gist: A costed ladder of certified rungs (140k, 150k, 165k, 175k, then 200k) under 10^200. The last e^5.5 would be closed by a few hundred volunteer GPUs for a quarter, an ASIC/FPGA rack, or a 10× fleet plus rounding mathematics, now measured at no more than 0.8 to 1.3 nats.
nodes.detail: Also priced: volunteer compute on the scale of Folding@home (about 2×10^5 times the fleet) would reach 200,000 in about two days; a Grover search is not competitive unless one oracle call takes seconds. The fleet's actual records (146,191, 157,837, 158,209, 160,357) followed the early rungs.

note.text: The plan the fleet then followed in practice: six record-setting finds in three days (22 to 24 Nov).

nodes.title: Decoding barrier: sub-100 digits is brute force or nothing
nodes.gist: Below 100 digits the conventional cover needs E = 44.1 (about 9×10^5 GPU-years). Oversized covers would make it easy, but finding their small representative is a modular subset-sum at density 1.026, and CRT list-decoding is blocked by the Johnson radius.
nodes.detail: A first version claimed an ‘open window’ for decoding; it compared bounds at different parameters, was retracted, and was replaced by a coupled barrier. Costed rungs: 140 digits needs 1.6×10^12 candidates (0.10 A100-years), 130 digits 3.6×10^13, 120 digits 1.2×10^15.

note.text: Not about the 200-digit budget game, but the origin of the decoding-barrier theory that the Lean library later formalised for the search problem.

nodes.title: Toy CRT decoder: LLL stops at the Johnson radius
nodes.gist: A lattice decoder (61 positions, B = 10^12) recovers a planted message only above about 1.028 times the Johnson radius, falling toward the radius as the lattice degree grows. Below it, no non-planted solution was ever found although 10² to 10⁷ are expected.
nodes.detail: 390 decodes with predeclared trials. It checks, on a case small enough to run, that practical lattice decoding does not exploit the abundance of solutions.

nodes.title: A proof of RH/GRH would move no lever
nodes.gist: Granting the claimed proof, RH and GRH give square-root-quality estimates, while every bottleneck lives at x^(o(1)) scale: the RH window would still fall short by 10^97 at the 200-digit record.
nodes.detail: GRH would only make Miller's test a proof (not competitive with elliptic-curve or BLS proofs) and change constants: the Linnik gain is a factor 1.2, after an erratum, not 2.5. The research sessions assumed the claim without examining its Lean archive.

note.text: Why only the method of the GRH note was used: find a toy over function fields, look for the integer counterpart, formalise as you go.

nodes.title: Theorem: covers reach 1.349 · x · ln x
nodes.gist: Residue classes modulo the odd primes up to x can cover every odd prime below (e^γ/(2C₂) − o(1))·x·ln x, so some explicit N has no Goldbach summand below 1.349·ln N·ln ln N.
nodes.detail: Proved on paper by pigeonhole, Mertens and one survivor per prime in (x/ln x, x]. It beats the thesis's bound by ln₃N/ln₄N and the counting constant 1/2 (Shi). Greedy covers track 0.72·x·ln²x, one logarithm higher; proving any f(x) → ∞ times x·ln x is the named open next theorem. Letting each mop-up prime cover two rows would double the constant, and several rows per prime would add a factor ln ln X / ln ln ln X; the research session states both only as remarks, proved neither there nor in Lean, which has the one-row-per-prime version. Since 24 Nov: a sketch for beating the constant exists (pairs of survivors struck by one large prime and a deletion argument, giving (1 + δ)·1.349 with δ about 0.1 measured; a Rödl nibble for any constant), certified covers reach 3.5 to 5 times the proved constant (up to 614,101 on 1,228 moduli), and the research session conjectures D(n) ≈ 1.1275 · r ln² r.

note.text: Kernel-checked in Lean as the covering bound with c < 1.349 and no hypothesis, with Mertens' third theorem proved in the same library.  Superseded in order on 25 Nov: a structured prefix gives r·ln² r·ln₃ r/(ln₂ r)² at paper level and r·ln² r/(9000 (ln₂ r)²) in the kernel (boxes ‘A structured prefix beats random classes’, ‘The order of the covering bound in the kernel’).

nodes.title: Theorem: no cover beyond x^(4+ε)
nodes.gist: For every ε > 0 and large x, classes modulo primes up to x cannot cover all primes below x^(4+ε), or x^(2+ε) under Elliott–Halberstam.
nodes.detail: By the linear sieve with Bombieri–Vinogradov. The first unconditional impossibility statement for covering certificates, but asymptotic and vacuous at record parameters (moduli up to 79,139 against Q up to 2×10^6). GRH adds nothing. A computed non-asymptotic bound at record size now exists too: D(89) < 35,000 by exhaustive search (4.6·10^8 nodes), and D(n) is known exactly to n = 35. Lean shows that depth below the next prime squared minus two for every n would imply Goldbach.

note.text: Brackets certified deserts between (1.349 − o(1))·ln N·ln ln N and (ln N)^(4+ε).

nodes.title: Unconditional growth: g ≫ ln N · ln₂N · ln₄N / ln₃N
nodes.gist: There are infinitely many even N with g(N) ≫ (log N)(log₂ N)(log₄ N)/log₃ N. The proof uses the Erdős–Rankin covering of an interval (Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao) with Linnik's size bound.
nodes.detail: This matches the best known prime-gap order. Between it and the conjectured (log N)² log log N lies a factor of about log N; whether covering only the prime offsets beats the prime-gap scale asymptotically would be new mathematics. It relies on external theorems and is not formalised. The research session conjectured on 24 Nov that divisibility by primes up to ln N forces a least summand of (1.1275 + o(1))·ln N·(ln ln N)²; it withdrew that on 25 Nov and now has the order ln N·(ln ln N)²/ln ln ln N (heuristic), which is not derived either. The least summand can be as large as c·ln N·(ln₂N)²·ln₄N/(ln₃N)² for infinitely many N at paper level, and ln N·(ln₂N)²/(150000 (ln₃N)²) in the kernel (boxes ‘A structured prefix beats random classes’, ‘The order of the covering bound in the kernel’), above the earlier proved order and below ln²N·ln ln N.

note.text: The rigorous lower end of the maximal order of g. The 1.349·ln N·ln ln N theorem is stronger by a log-ratio.

nodes.title: Thesis chapter 2: the classical constructions
nodes.gist: A factorial leaves one residue class per small prime. A multiple of the primorial has no small summands. A congruence cover needs only 356 congruences and a 1,020-digit modulus for Q = 10^5, against a primorial of 43,000 digits. Every cover is realised by true Goldbach numbers (Dirichlet). A prime gap gives a Goldbach gap, but not conversely.
nodes.detail: Worked example: N = 27! + 28 (29 digits) has g = 71. A complete greedy cover for Q = 10^8 would need about 327,455 digits.

note.text: These are the paper's statements; the Lean library proves them (primorial core, covering certificate, cover realisation, Dirichlet existence with and without Linnik, prime-gap transfer).

nodes.title: N − 1 (BLS) certificate by CRT: no ECPP
nodes.gist: Choose N by CRT so that P = N − g equals m·2ⁿ + 1 with 2ⁿ at least P^(1/3). One modular exponentiation and an integer square root then prove P prime (Brillhart–Lehmer–Selfridge). With a complete cover, g(N) = g is certified with no luck, no ECPP and no heuristic.
nodes.detail: The price is about 1.5 times the digits. Found independently by two sessions. It removed the height game's certification wall (the ECPP-limited ceiling had been forecast at 2.5 million). It needs a complete cover, which under the 10^200 cap stops near 16,000, so it is not used for the budget game.

nodes.gist: Research proposed that a record should carry a machine-checkable proof: a decidable check that every prime below g is covered or fails a Fermat test, plus a primality certificate for N − g. The Lean session built exactly that for the budget game.

nodes.gist: If rows-left is normal across candidates and success probability is (1 − p)^R, the candidates at least z standard deviations below the mean hold the fraction Φ(λ − z) of all successes. The identity is exact for the normal.
nodes.detail: Measured on 131,072 members of a Q = 130,000 vector: the emptiest 8% hold 23.7% of the hit mass against 24.3% by the model; the fleet's 3% rule holds 15.6%, worth 2.0 nats. The model is 5–10% optimistic in the tail.

nodes.title: The 200-idea brainstorm: nothing worth a nat
nodes.gist: On 2026-11-22 the two sessions each wrote 100 ideas for a large step at 200 digits and tested each other's. None is worth a nat as a change of method; what is left is engineering (0.6–1.3 nats) and compute.

The Lean session settled 21 of the ideas by theorem; a refuted claim (‘E ≥ 33 for every modulus set’) shows the exchange ran in both directions. nodes.title: Retractions and errata
nodes.gist: Claims walked back so far: an ‘open window’ for CRT decoding (WP3), a factor-10 units slip in the sub-100 cost, two ‘independent’ unlucky searches that were one event (p = 0.046), ‘first record without ECPP’ (it was an independent second certificate), GRH's gain of 2.5 (really 1.2), Theorem 2 as practical (asymptotic only), the fitted ceiling constant, and fail-open PARI scripts.
nodes.detail: Each was found by cross-review or by recomputation, and none changed a record. Still open in the ledgers: a campaign-1 ‘P ≈ 0.30’ that the log's own table puts near 0.09; the 57-versus-68-nat entropy arithmetic in WP3; and the claim that the model is within 0.1 nats when campaign 3's log is 0.2–0.4 above. Added since: the soft-threshold conclusion of the brainstorm README (retracted); the D(n) counts for n = 25 to 27 (withdrawn after an array overflow, rerun with the same answers); the law's limit constant (1.349, then open, then 1.1275 within two hours, and since qualified by the referee check); marks per N at 170,000 (83, then 68); 4,500 corrected to 4,700 digits for a forced gap of 10^6; the planning horizon (8.5 and 8.2 days corrected to 8.9; 29M to 52M members a second); the entropy-zero plateau estimate (about 10 rows early at 170,000). On this map: the primality chains are 26 steps for 158,209 and 21 for 160,357 (the first version of the map said 27), and the earlier ladder's range is 17 to 31 steps.

nodes.title: The sublinear search question (P′)
nodes.gist: Can we find, faster than scoring every candidate, an N below 10^200 with at most 1,320 of the primes q < 213,070 having N − q free of prime factors up to 1,000? About e^36 such N exist; the best covers give 1,439 ± 11.
nodes.detail: A solution would be worth 3.5 nats (a factor 30) at the 10% target. The programme began on 2026-11-23, taking only the method from the GRH note: find a function-field toy, look for the integer counterpart, formalise as you go.

note.text: The one open door of the brainstorm, and the whole sublinear programme.

nodes.title: What a perfect search would be worth
nodes.gist: An ideal search at the 10% target would need to test e^39.3 numbers per success today, e^35.8 if it could see rows to depth 1,000, e^30.5 for depth 5,000 and e^26.7 for 20,000. The prize is 3.5, 5.9, 8.8, 12.6 and 14.8 nats for depths 1,000 to 50,000.
nodes.detail: Computed by tempering plus multi-histogram reweighting over residue vectors (108 temperatures), assuming numbers below 10^200 are a fair sample of the vectors. With the remaining budget of e^30.75, an ideal search to depth 5,000 would reach 214,000 (10.0%) and to depth 20,000 would reach 235,000. About 10^175 numbers qualify at 10%, one in 10^25: the difficulty is entirely location. The extension to depth 10^8 treats rows beyond the cut-off as independent; Lean's thinning law shows that can only make the ideal search look cheaper than it is. The 1/ln² z regularity of the table is explained: if the primes between two depths kill rows independently the deep table is the shallow one at another temperature (Lean's thinning law proves independence a safe direction above Q, and the table's depths lie below Q), and rows fall like (ln z)^−a with a = 2.0 to 2.1 (measured β 1.22 to 1.32); the whole table follows from one shallow table within 0.4 nats from depth 5,000. The prize is the same function as the floor under covers.

nodes.title: Barrier: free coordinates stop at the cap
nodes.gist: By the Chinese remainder theorem the residues modulo primes whose product is at most 10^200 can be prescribed, and N is then determined. Beyond that line the landscape is a random-energy model, so there are no local moves.
nodes.detail: The odd primes up to 463 and 2 multiply to 10^192.67, so the 460.5 nats of 10^200 just suffice to pin the primes up to 463: enumerating covers best-first is already an ideal search to depth 463. Lean: two numbers below X agreeing modulo M and every s in T satisfy M·∏T < X; with X ≤ M·463⁴ at most three sieve primes can be kept.

nodes.title: Barrier: lattices and CRT with errors or lists
nodes.gist: Chinese remaindering with errors finds N only when lists are short and agreement is high: the decoding radius is about four times the typical agreement, while the best member among K exceeds the typical one by a few percent.
nodes.detail: For the 580 primes from 467 to 5,000 with one-class lists in a population of e^83, the best agreement that exists is about 22 against a radius of 78. Lean proves the radius is at least 3.88 times the typical agreement for K = 2³², and that informative lists lie outside it. A later attack on this barrier (LATTICE_CHECK.md) recomputed it on another cover, simulated a whole window and tried hard lists, soft weights (closed form ratio² ≤ ln(1 + n/x)/ln K), subsets, products and per-prime exponents: the best decoder reaches 0.36 of the agreement it needs. The claim stands.

nodes.title: Barrier: meet in the middle, birthday trees, hashing
nodes.gist: A meet-in-the-middle yields solutions at constant cost each only when the list entropy H ≤ 2(F − C). For the whole problem and a memory of e^21 it extends the reach by one prime, worth about 0.2 nats. Locality-sensitive hashing gets at best K^0.94.
nodes.detail: The measured instance is the joint representative construction, which cancelled 24.3 digits of modulus at the price of the search entropy. Two independent derivations give hashing exponents 0.88 and 0.99.

note.text: Going past the line by enumeration is possible, but only one prime at a time.

nodes.title: Barrier: linear-time scoring is optimal
nodes.gist: What remains is to score every member (the fleet's sieve does it at 23 ns each). The gain of selection depends only on the kept fraction, and the sieve cannot skip members because marks are generated along progressions.
nodes.detail: Lean bounds: m questions to a black box reach the fraction m·g/K of the target set, and a perfect solver on the present progressions is worth at most 4.3–5.3 nats over the 3% rule for a population of e^22. Lattices of moves, additive and multiplicative splittings, tree search with bounds, polynomial parametrisations and row sharing by convolution were tried without success. The optimality statement itself is a conjecture. Measured on exhaustive data: no other function of the same residues predicts a success better than the count of rows left (see 'Tested: no score beats the survivor count'). Row sharing by convolution is now priced: with the primes of a stretch known a number needs about 68 marks, four times cheaper per number but a million times worse per operation, and it excludes covers (see ‘Neighbouring N share the prime map’).

nodes.title: Barrier: list gain above Q is tiny
nodes.gist: For one prime s, any list of classes gains at most (W − μ)/ln(W/μ) rows per nat of constraint. For primes above Q (W = 1, at most 1,609 rows) that is 0.207 rows, or 0.005 nats of success, per nat spent: six times less than an extra covering prime.
nodes.detail: So nothing that enumerates a product of lists collects the part of the prize above Q. For arbitrary lists, ‘does any N below a bound meet every list’ is NP-complete already with two classes per modulus (Manders–Adleman).

nodes.title: Exact miniature: N below 10^9, Q = 1,000
nodes.gist: A testbed small enough to enumerate: among the 157,947,020 even N below 10^9 with no prime factor from 3 to 29, exactly 256 have g ≥ 1,000. Ordering by rows left at depth 200 finds the first success after 13 numbers; ‘cover first’ needs 2,982.
nodes.detail: The tilt prediction matches the exact count within 3% where counts are large. The best numbers are independent needles, with no structure tying one to another (correlation −0.029). The Lean session's independent re-enumeration gave the same joint histogram byte for byte. Lean then showed that needles closer than Q share rows, so they are not independent. Seven mechanisms outside the closure grammar were scored on this miniature and on two variants (N below 2·10⁹; Q = 900), each out of sample: see the box ‘Seven mechanisms outside the closure grammar, scored on the exact miniature’.

nodes.title: Function-field toy: a parity desert, formally proved
nodes.gist: Over F_q[x] with q an odd square, N = λ·V^p (V the product of all irreducibles up to degree J, λ a non-square) makes N − Q reducible for every irreducible Q up to degree J + 1. The extra degree comes from a parity theorem proved with Stickelberger–Swan.
nodes.detail: The Lean session derived the parity theorem independently as one identity over any field and gave, as far as either session knows, the first formal proof of Stickelberger–Swan. It also found two extensions (any degree; smooth derivative). Checked by factoring over F_3 to F_49 in every case tried.
nodes.search: function field parity desert stickelberger swan toy

note.text: The proof of concept that a compositeness mechanism that is neither a small factor nor luck exists, in a toy. The mechanism is classical (Swan 1962; Conrad–Conrad–Gross; Sawin–Shusterman).

nodes.title: Toy search over F₃[x]: the parity filter is worth 4–5×
nodes.gist: A full search in the toy (greedy cover on the 14 irreducibles of degree ≤ 3, 1,318 rows, members of degree 93) shows half the rows have odd parity and no irreducible N − Q has even parity. Testing only odd rows at the best 3% of members gives 4.5 times more successes per test.
nodes.detail: That is 1.4–1.6 nats: a constant factor, with every member still looked at. Counting also settles desert versus cover: an ordinary cover equals the desert at degree J + 1 and beats it above, so the toy's lesson is ‘use an ordinary cover, a generic N, and the parity filter on what is left’.

nodes.title: Why the integers are harder: a known non-analogy
nodes.gist: The integer counterpart would compute or force the parity of the number of prime factors of N − q. But λ(n) has no formula short of factoring, and congruence information is uncorrelated with λ by the parity problem of sieve theory.
nodes.detail: Every algebraic certificate tried exhibits a factorisation costing a congruence per row. Genus theory gives an integer shadow (the number of prime factors is the 2-rank of a class group plus one) but reading it means finding ambiguous forms, as hard as factoring. The function-field mechanism is the standard ‘non-analogy’ example (K. Conrad).

note.text: Names the new mathematics that would be needed: an integer parity filter, the counterpart of H2.

nodes.title: The sublinear programme's ladder
nodes.gist: Nine rungs: (1) toy theorem with formal proof, done; (2) toy search with the parity filter, done; (3) a fully enumerable toy, done over the integers (not in F_q[x]); (4) formal barrier statements for the integer search, done; (5) integer information that is not a residue, open; (6) wheel and list merges, costed at 0.1–0.4 nats; (7) the ideal-search prize, done; (8) problem (P′), open; (9) a provable lower bound for pure covers, done (16,981).
nodes.detail: The programme's own account of what is proved, measured and open, as of 2026-11-25.

nodes.title: Sublinear verdict so far: none known, none ruled out
nodes.gist: A third compositeness mechanism exists in the toy (worth 4–5×, or 1.4–1.6 nats). Over the integers a perfect search would win 3.5–14.8 nats. Beyond the Chinese-remainder line, lattices, list decoding, meet-in-the-middle, birthday trees and hashing are ruled out with numbers, and linear-time scoring is at its optimum.
nodes.detail: Nothing proves that no sublinear algorithm exists. Still open: (P′), the fully enumerable toy, non-residue information (equal to H2) and constants worth 0.1–0.4 nats. The research session has since corrected the README (commit 02564fb): ‘about e^10’ now names an explicit family and points to the count of about e^27 at depth 10^8, and the cost exponent between neighbouring targets runs from 1.2 to 2.3, not 1.4 to 1.8. Update of 25 Nov: still none known, none ruled out. By measurement the covers in use are the best there are (better covers are not a way to 10%); the numbers wanted exist (about 10^175 even N below 10^200 have g ≥ 213,070) but 10^200 only pins residues up to 463; a perfect search at the fleet's sieve depth stops near 16% of the ceiling. New: the SAT reduction for arbitrary rows, row sharing priced and found incompatible with covers, and no lower bound against algorithms on prime rows from any known technique.

note.text: As of 25 November: the prize is real and of known size, covers collect all of it below the line, and above it every known method costs more than scoring members one by one.

nodes.title: Tested: the chance that every row is composite
nodes.gist: Group the numbers by how many rows survive a sieve to depth z. Once z is past the threshold, the model's (1 − c)^rows matches the observed share of big numbers to within about 1% wherever the counts are large, over five orders of magnitude of probability and at all three scales.
nodes.detail: This is the joint event 'all rows composite' itself, conditional on the sieve: what H1's own text says a first-moment match does not pin down. Observed against predicted totals for z = 997, 9,973 and 65,521 are 0.993 to 1.005 at the three scales. With a sieve shallower than the threshold (z = 13 or 97) the model expects 2–9% too many big numbers, with the sign and size of the pair term in the fscan notes. Past the threshold the two agree to within the noise, as the thinning law's inequality and its small gap estimate suggest. A later, independent check on real data (BOTTOM_UP.md section 5): the same independent-rows model, with a cover as the class vector modulo the small primes, reproduces the inter-record times of the 69 published records of the least Goldbach summand (OEIS A025018/A025019): an excess of +0.06 ± 0.34 nats for N from 8·10¹³ to 9·10¹⁷ (exponent 30 to 40 nats), 0.6 to 0.9 nats optimistic below 5·10¹³.

nodes.title: Tested: pairs of neighbours at 366 lags
nodes.gist: For every even lag d up to 732: how much likelier N + d is to be big when N is big. The model predicts each lag from shared rows and residues alone: within about 1% at the strong lags (multiples of 6, about 18 times at d = 30) and within the error bars everywhere.

N + d reuses the composite N − q whenever q and q + d are both prime: at d = 30 that is 67 of the 111 rows near 10^18. An apparent 3–5% excess at lags ≡ 2 (mod 6) did not survive block-bootstrap error bars: 1.05 ± 0.09 near 10^18 and 1.00 ± 0.07 near 10^15.

nodes.title: Archipelagos: big gaps come in clusters
nodes.gist: Link big numbers that share at least a quarter of their rows: 86–91% of them belong to a cluster, an archipelago. Near 10^18 the largest has 176 members and sits on the largest prime gap in the 40-million-number window (558). Clusters of 20 or more are 26 times as common as in a control that keeps every residue effect of 2 to 13.
nodes.detail: Each archipelago sits above a prime-poor stretch: the 176-member one above 1,152 numbers that hold only eight primes. Each extra prime among the 614 numbers below N multiplies the chance of a big gap by about 0.72. Clustering fades as the level rises: the share of exceedances that start a new cluster is 0.10 at the top 1%, 0.50 at the top 0.1% and 0.80 at the top 0.01%. What the neighbours can give at the campaign's cover is bounded: the success mass of all neighbours is 3.6% of the member's own there, a ceiling of +0.035 nats (box ‘Neighbours of near-successes’).

nodes.title: Who the big numbers are
nodes.gist: Near 10^18 only 0.9% of big numbers are divisible by 3, against a third of all numbers, and 57.4% are ≡ 2 (mod 3) against 41.7% ≡ 1. Below 614 there are 57 primes ≡ 2 (mod 3) and 53 ≡ 1, so N ≡ 2 kills four more rows. The same tilt toward quadratic non-residues shows mod 5 and mod 7.

nodes.title: The exact search for D(n): one lemma, several cuts
nodes.gist: Branch on the least unstruck prime and try each unused modulus. What makes it fast is one lemma (in a vector that beats the best so far, every free modulus sits in a class within the margin of its fullest class) plus a capacity count. The proof for 35 moduli takes 9·10^9 nodes and an hour.

Checks: two child orders, brute force up to nine moduli, a SAT solver (unsatisfiable for n = 9 to 12, with proof files written but no proof checker run), each cut switched off, and counts from several programs. An array overflow in the build used for n = 25 to 27 was found by the uarch session's large-neighbourhood search; the three counts were withdrawn on 24 Nov and rerun with identical answers. A large-neighbourhood search around the 15,907 cover on 89 moduli (freeing up to 32 of them) found no improvement: the cover is locally rigid.

At the design level Q = 170,000 it also proves that every vector leaves at least 777 of the 15,496 odd primes unstruck.

No-cover proofs: Y = 170,000 in 0.2 s, 45,000 in 12 s, 37,000 in 512 s, 35,000 in 4.6·10^8 nodes and an hour (stopped by choice). Floors with the first j moduli fixed in every way: 401 (j = 6), 644 (j = 8), 777 (j = 10, 7.3·10^8 nodes, 3.5 hours). The best cover known leaves 1,248, so 777 is 62% of it and the theorem still allows about 11 nats; two more fixed moduli multiply the work by 40 to 160. A different bound, for fixed small classes, gives 1,170 rows (a linear programme over the other 67 moduli), valid only for the 22 small classes of the best cover. The 89-moduli proofs have one implementation; the reading agent re-derived the floors for j = 4 to 7 with its own program but did not re-run the proof at 35,000 or the floors for j = 8 and 10.

Leaving the classes up to x^0.6 to chance costs 5 to 12% of the reach. On 167 moduli a planned (tempered) assignment leaves nothing below 40,111 where greedy leaves 33, and its 56 largest moduli strike 1.38 times the independent-cell maximum.

The walls at the smallest sizes are the true optima (D(30) = 2,311 and D(34) = 2,953 are the exhaustive values), but from x = 397 on the successful runs used 50 to 97% of their budget, so the entries from x = 349 are budget-limited lower bounds; the research recursion puts the end for x = 1,499 and 1,999 (238 and 302 moduli) near 1.0 · x ln² x, so the covers found are 85 to 88% of it. nodes.title: The law derived: a price per alive row, with the spread from Hardy–Littlewood pairs
nodes.gist: Count the covers one modulus at a time, smallest first. Each alive row carries a price p, and the price before a modulus s is the price after it minus κ(p)/(s − 1), κ = (e^(vp) − 1)/v, where v is the variance-to-mean ratio of the alive rows per class; Poisson rows (v = 1) give the first-moment count. The measured spread, computed from Hardy–Littlewood prime-pair sums, gives the law with nothing fitted.
nodes.detail: The pair weight is W(j) = a·c·∏(1 + u_t) with u_t = 2/(t − 3) below the modulus and 1/(t − 2) above; the Lean session proves its exact mean 6s/(s − 1), its product form, and that partial sums never exceed the mean. Tests: loss within 5% at the first nine sizes (x from 463 to 9,973, that is 89 to 1,228 moduli); measured over predicted 0.96 to 1.05 at 30 to 108 moduli; ends within 4% of the best cover known from 20 to 89 moduli; a prediction put on record before the runs at x = 797, 1,499 and 1,999 (138, 238 and 302 moduli) came out at 0.975 to 1.04. At 1,228 moduli the range 3,330 to 3,414 was on record first and the runs give 3,438 to 3,467 from above (one-sided: a finite run overestimates the loss); the point figure 3,394 was written after a long run had been pushed. As first written the recursion lets the small moduli choose classes they have not the entropy to choose, and its limit 1.1275 was withdrawn on 25 Nov; the version with that entropy put in is the next box.

nodes.title: Why 1.349 is not the truth: pairs, deletion and the nibble
nodes.gist: After random classes on the small primes, each large prime can strike two or more survivors: two survivors in one class of a large prime r are primes q, q′ with r dividing q′ − q. A deletion argument (keep a random part of such pairs, drop conflicts) gives (1 + δ)·1.349; any constant would need a near-perfect matching of the pair hypergraph (a Rödl nibble). Neither is written out.
nodes.detail: Measured by the archipelago session (x = 3,000 to 10^6): survivors match the first-moment count within 1%; pairs are 0.38 to 0.87 of the independent-balls count (survivors are capped, thinned targets); the second moment is at most 1.26 times mean² and conflicts match independent degrees (about 4); deletion keeps 9 to 14% of large primes, so the constant would be about 1.5, not 2. With random small classes up to x^0.9 and the fullest class above, everything is struck up to C = 1.39, 1.93, 2.47, 3.14 and 4.47 times x ln x at x = 3·10³, 10⁴, 3·10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶, still rising; all-greedy reaches 5.5 to 10. A correction found on the way: the pair count is zero at the prime 3 unless the rows agree mod 3 (all survivors lie in the one class mod 3 left unstruck), and the corrected pair step is a lower bound within 0.99 to 1.15 of the measurement.

nodes.title: A model with no primes in it reproduces the campaign's ceiling
nodes.gist: The Lean session replaced “is N − q prime?” by a probability from the Hardy–Littlewood density, plus one fitted correction for the dependence between the summands of one N. With that single constant, fitted on counts below 10^12, the formula reproduces the research team's figures for numbers below 10^200 to within 0.1 nats at five targets, and gives a ceiling of 2,133,689 against their 2,130,704.
nodes.detail: The chance that N is unstruck by the first m odd primes is (1 − h)^m · exp(−c · A_m · m · h²) with h = 2C₂ S(N)/ln N and c = 0.92. Tests not used in the fit: the counts up to 10^11 (within 5% up to m = 240) and the stretch from one record holder to the next up to 10^18 (expected number of unstruck numbers in it 1.00 ± 0.13 against 1; 11.6 for independent strikers). A forecast of when the next record holder falls puts 53 of 59 next terms inside its 5% to 95% band (53.1 expected). A generator run from 98 produces 63 further numbers to 4·10^18 that keep pace with the real sequence in count and size, but none of them is a real term.

So at most 0.8 nat is left in better covers at the campaign's level and 1.3 at the 10% target. A 1% chance of the 10% record would need about 1,470 rows by the planning model, 84 below the floor. nodes.title: The GPU sieve chain: a window's sieve phase from 83.7 to 44 ms
nodes.gist: In one day the sieve phase of a 2^24 window on the RTX PRO 6000 fell from 83.7 ms to 44.4 ms and a batch from 0.945 s to about 0.732 s: a factor 1.29 in rate, worth about +0.26 nats (about +1,200 in g).
nodes.detail: The steps: packed bins, hoisted loops and prefetch; flat flush and grid order; generate unroll 4 with clamped loads; a bundle of three sieve options named LEAN (−1.5 ms); a one-pass generate kernel that visits each (prime, row) pair once (generate 28.75 → 22.15 ms against an estimate of 17 to 21). A batch is the sieve time plus the Fermat time, not hidden behind it (batch = 0.371 + 37.97·(1 − f) s), so a millisecond off a window is worth up to four off a batch. The L4s and the T4 got the same stack (L4 batch ×0.850, T4 ×0.907). Measured and declined: near-miss truncation (×1.063 near-misses but ×0.937 design hits, declined by the lead), and a survivor-list kernel (0.6% of a batch, shelved). Failed predictions are part of the record: the L4 keep-fraction test (predicted ×1.13, measured ×1.0001, or ×0.98 to 0.99 against the drifting controls) and the one-pass estimate.

nodes.title: IFMA Fermat tests for 300 to 400 digits (8 to 12 times gmpy2)
nodes.gist: The 13-limb AVX-512 IFMA kernel that tests numbers up to 664 bits is generalised to any limb count (numbers up to 52L − 12 bits): 34.6 µs a test at 1,028 bits against 401 µs for gmpy2 (11.6×), 105.7 µs against 857 µs at 1,340 bits (8.1×).
nodes.detail: On a 400-digit g ≥ 200,000 cover (1,010 rows, 65,536 members) the scan statistics equal gmpy2's (42,483 tests, 1,312 probable primes) at 10,789 members a second instead of 1,874. The commit also says the older CPU path used the 13-limb kernel at any size, “which is wrong above 664 bits”: a 200-digit member can have 665 bits (the record's N is 9.53·10^199), and whether an earlier CPU-share run tested members above 664 bits is not stated. Hits are re-verified on gmpy2, so a false positive is caught but a missed hit would not be. Not re-run by the reading agent.

nodes.title: The other direction: a fixed gap and the fewest digits
nodes.gist: A number of size e^L carries the odd primes up to about L as moduli; the best cover leaves a fraction ρ(D/Q) of the rows that random classes leave, so one member in e^E succeeds with E = 2C₂·(π(Q)/L)·ρ(κ L ln² L/Q), and E is zero once D(L) ≥ Q. The model prices what a given gap needs in digits.
nodes.detail: Gap 200,000: members per success 10^15.4 at 200 digits (1,474 rows), 10^12.0 at 240, 10^8.6 at 300, 10^0.5 at 1,000; forced by divisibility from about 1,300 digits; a gap of 200,000 costs at about 230 digits what 170,000 costs at 200 (the same units would buy one expected success at about 225 digits). Gap 1,000,000: 10^37.4 at 400 digits down to 10^0.2 at 4,000; forced from about 4,700 digits (corrected from 4,500). The best known N with g above 10^6 had 2,480 digits and has 2,196 since 25 Nov at 12:12 (box ‘Fixed-gap records’). The predictions are untested far from 200 digits: the game was proposed on 25 Nov, and the first cover found for it (629 moduli) leaves 31% more rows than the table says.

nodes.title: A draft proof of a constant above 1.349: one prime striking two rows
nodes.gist: The sketch of the previous box made rigorous at paper level, at the research session's request: after random classes on the primes up to y/ln y, match survivors in pairs, each pair struck by one prime of (αy, y] that divides the difference of the two primes (a rainbow matching), and bound the matching by a deletion argument. With Lavrik-type Hardy–Littlewood for shifts of size about x and Selberg's upper bound for triples it gives classes striking every odd prime below c·y·ln y for every c below 1.3523, against the proved 1.3490.
nodes.detail: The survival weights of stage 1 cancel the Hardy–Littlewood singular series exactly (the identity C₂·∏(1 + 2/(p(p − 3)))·∏(1 − 1/(p − 2)²)·4/3 = 1 holds prime by prime), so the number of edges is what independent rows would give. The gain is small because Selberg's constant 48 for the triple count bounds the conflicts: the matching covers about 0.25% of the survivors. If every second moment had its predicted value the same argument would give 1.479, which agrees with the measured deletion fractions of the archipelago session (1.48 to 1.51). Named gaps: the precise form of the long-range almost-all theorem (Mikawa's range as quoted in the literature does not contain shifts that large; Lavrik's and Wolke's should), an averaging lemma for the weights over prime labels (outline only), and ineffective constants. Not formalisable in Lean.

nodes.title: A structured prefix beats random classes: D(n) ≥ c·r·ln² r·ln₃ r/(ln₂ r)²
nodes.gist: Give every modulus in a block of primes (z, x/4] the class of one common integer N₁ near Q. A row q survives only if N₁ − q has no prime factor in the block, which leaves O(ln ln x/ln x) of the rows where random classes leave ln z/ln x (the Erdős–Rankin device). With each prime up to z taking its fullest class and each prime above x/4 striking one row, it gives a depth of at least c·r·ln² r·ln₃ r/(ln₂ r)², more than every constant times r ln r. The Lean session has since proved it in the kernel for every constant and with the order r·ln² r/(9000·(ln₂ r)²), that is without the factor ln₃, which remains on paper. The same prefix breaks the premise of the limit arguments (the small moduli can do no better than random classes), so the ratio D/(x ln² x) is not shown to tend to 0, and 1.1275 and its replacement r ln² r/ln ln r are both not derived.
nodes.detail: Found by the Lean session's second referee read (25 Nov, about 11:20 UTC); the lower bound was written out line by line by the consultant (COHERENT_BLOCK.md): averaging over N₁ in (Q, 2Q] (counting the integers below 2Q with no prime factor in the block) needs only Chebyshev, Mertens and a Rankin-type bound for smooth numbers, with ln z = ln x·ln₃x/(3 ln₂x). Exact counts (Lean): the block (406, 937,500] at Q = 6·10⁷ leaves 32.3% of the rows against 44.0% for random classes; the ratio falls from 0.98 at ln x = 9.2 to 0.55 at 50, 0.37 at 100 and 0.07 at 1000 (half as many only near x = 10²⁵). Consultant's counts on real primes: 0.93, 0.86, 0.72, 0.57 at x = 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶, 3.75·10⁶. With the block the count for the top primes forbids nothing below about x·ln³x·ln₃x/(3(ln₂x)³) (not a claim that covers exist there). At the sizes in reach nothing changes: a cover built from the block, greedy small moduli and greedy top primes reaches 0.39 to 0.48·x ln² x at x = 10⁴ against 0.71 for plain greedy. Through the Chinese remainder theorem: infinitely many even N have no Goldbach summand below c·ln N·(ln₂N)²·ln₄N/(ln₃N)².

nodes.title: A referee's second read of the entropy of the small moduli
nodes.gist: The Lean session reimplemented the constrained recursion from its description and reproduced all 24 rows of the research table. It finds (a) the identity right but the dispersion at the smallest moduli not nearly 0 (0.058, 0.057, 0.054 at 3, 5, 7 from the primes, against −0.18, −0.07, −0.003 from the pair sum), which moves every figure by 1 to 6%; (b) the family of constraints necessary inside the model but not settled by it (the recursion depends on the order of the moduli); (c) the dual correct; (d) the argument for the limit not holding: the small moduli can be set outside the model's distribution, and a common-integer block leaves far fewer rows than random classes.
nodes.detail: (b) At 1,228 moduli and Q = 300,000 the recursion gives a loss of 3,349 in increasing order, 3,452 with the six smallest moduli first and the rest in decreasing order, and 1,606 in decreasing order (measured at most 3,438). With the dispersions from the primes the agreement in the middle of the range improves (measured over constrained 0.984 to 1.003 against 0.945 to 0.99) and near the end it is worse (1.02 to 1.04 against 0.99 to 1.016): a rise of 5 to 6% from the middle to the end that the constraint does not remove, and what is missing acts toward fewer covers near the end. (c) Weak duality is immediate and strong duality holds, checked numerically (a direct maximisation at 89 moduli agrees to 10⁻⁹). (d) The block leaves 2% fewer rows than random classes at x = 10⁴ and 9% fewer at 10⁶, half as many only near 10²⁵; at x = 9,973 the constrained count (1.0 · x ln² x) does better than either the block or random classes below the top (about 0.6). So at the sizes that can be computed nothing changes and every statement about the limit does.

nodes.title: The covering bound for every constant, in the kernel
nodes.gist: For every real A and all large X there is an even N ≤ X, larger than A·ln X·ln ln X, such that no q < A·ln X·ln ln X is a Goldbach summand of N: the largest least Goldbach summand below X is not O(ln X ln ln X). The cover has three layers: the primes in (z, y/4] all take the class of one common integer N₁ (the Erdős–Rankin block), the odd primes up to z take their fullest class, and the primes in (y/4, y] strike one row each. N₁ is not fixed but averaged over [Q, 2Q), so the count is a count of integers: Rankin's bound for the smooth ones, the prime number theorem and a harmonic sum for the others.
nodes.detail: Files CoverEveryConstant.lean (1,316 lines) and Cap/CommonInteger.lean (295 lines). Main statements: eventually_exists_even_le_every_constant, eventually_exists_classes_every_constant (classes on the odd primes up to y striking every odd prime below A·y·ln y) and CoverCount.eventually_g0_pos_every_constant. The combinatorial step is Cap.exists_common_integer (an N₁ in [Q, 2Q) whose block leaves at most the share of the integers below 2Q with no prime factor in the block), with Cap.card_no_factor_le, Cap.card_smooth_le_exp (Rankin's bound) and eventually_card_smooth_le; the passage from the cover to the number N is eventually_exists_even_le_of_stage. The pigeonhole layer is the odd primes up to z = ⌊ln y⌋^K − 1 with K = ⌈300A⌉ + 1. The library's note says every theorem depends on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound only; a text search of the three files finds no sorry, native_decide or added axiom (I did not run Lean).

nodes.title: The order of the covering bound in the kernel: ln X·(ln ln X)²/(150000·(ln ln ln X)²)
nodes.gist: Letting the exponent K grow with y (K = ⌊ln y/(14 (ln ln y)²)⌋, so that z is a power of y with exponent about 1/(14 ln ln y)), the same cover has depth at least y·ln² y/(9000·(ln ln y)²), and the largest least Goldbach summand below X is at least ln X·(ln ln X)²/(150000·(ln ln ln X)²) for all large X. This is Rankin's order for prime gaps with one more logarithm, short of the paper-level bound of the consultant's note by the factor ln₃: the smooth numbers are counted with e^(−u) where the sharp count has u^(−u).
nodes.detail: Statements: eventually_exists_even_le_log; eventually_exists_classes_log (classes striking every odd prime below ⌊y ln² y/(9000 (ln ln y)²)⌋); CoverCount.eventually_g0_pos_log (the number of complete covers there is positive). Technical lemmas: card_smooth_le_of_log_le (Rankin's bound with σ = 1 − 1/ln N), exists_sum_primesLE_inv_le (Mertens' bound ∑_{p≤w} 1/p ≤ ln ln w + K₀) and eventually_logA_bounds. The constants 9000 and 150000 are what the crude steps leave and mean nothing. What is not proved is the last factor: with ln z = ln y·ln₃y/(3 ln₂y) and the sharp count the same cover gives c·y·ln² y·ln₃ y/(ln₂ y)² rows.

nodes.title: Fixed-gap records: 347 digits for a gap above 200,000, 2,196 digits for a million
nodes.gist: The fixed-gap game fixes the bound and asks for the fewest digits: an even N with N − q composite for every prime q below the bound. Three records are in the Lean kernel, found by the exact-search session on CPUs: 400 digits with no Goldbach summand below 200,293 and below 206,593, and 347 digits with none below 216,289. For a gap of 1,000,000 the Opus session found a 2,196-digit N with g ≥ 1,001,491 (25 Nov, 12:12), replacing the 2,480-digit height-game record; the research session rechecked it from N alone and its certificate is in progress. Numbers of about 319 and 300 digits for a gap of 200,000 are running.
nodes.detail: The statements are the negative side only: for every prime q below the bound N − q is divisible by one of the cover's moduli or fails the base-2 Fermat test, so no primality proof is involved and the exact least summand is not claimed. For the 347-digit N: 19,307 primes below 216,289; for 18,038 of them one of the 141 covering moduli (3 to 821) divides N − q, and for the other 1,269 it fails the Fermat test. Lean: exists_400_digit_no_summand_below_200293 and …_206593 and the 347-digit statement in FixedGap.lean, with the certificate files Gap200k_*. The 400-digit records took under two CPU-hours. Whether the records agree with the model of the box ‘The other direction’ (which priced a gap of 200,000 at 10^8.6 members per success at 300 digits) is not assessed here.

nodes.title: The recursion with the entropy of the small moduli put in: the ends move by 1 to 2% and the ratio turns down
nodes.gist: In the research session's recursion the class chosen at a modulus s holds e^(v·t) times the mean number of alive rows, which exists only if the smaller moduli have arranged it, and that costs entropy. Summed over a prefix of the moduli the entropy cannot be negative, but in the recursion it is (down to −8 nats at 89 moduli and −219 at 1,228). Requiring every prefix to have entropy ≥ 0 (a convex minimisation: the same recursion with weights w ≥ 1) freezes the small moduli, whose classes then agree in nearly all complete covers: the families of the long runs. The predicted end of complete covers moves by 1 to 2%, and D/(x ln² x) peaks near 1.0 at about a thousand moduli and turns down.
nodes.detail: D/(x ln² x) with the constraint, against the recursion as first written: 0.912 (x = 463), 0.929 (797), 0.944 (997), 0.975 (1,499), 0.975 (1,999), 0.988 (2,999), 1.008 (9,973), 0.995 (30,000), 0.982 (100,000), 0.960 (300,000), 0.936 (10⁶), that is 89 to 78,497 moduli, against 0.913, 0.933, 0.952, 0.991, 0.995, 1.019, 1.074, 1.097, 1.125, 1.140, 1.154. Found or counted: 0.912 found at 89 moduli, 0.923 to 0.926 at 138 (counts extended), 0.876 found at 167, 0.970 to 0.973 at 238 and at least 0.956 at 302 (counts extended). The last three columns were computed by a contractor session with the same script. The test left open on 24 Nov (1,228 moduli, Q = 300,000): 3,452 with the constraint and 3,409 without, against runs that read 3,465 at 150,000 sweeps and 3,438 at 500,000, still falling; the README says this decides nothing between the two. The figures move by about 1% with the cut of the dispersion at the moduli 3 to 17 (the end on 89 moduli is 15,907, 16,063 or 16,218 for cuts 10⁻⁴, 0.02 and 0.06, against 15,907 found), so the constrained recursion is a 1 to 2% statement about where complete covers end, and an exact treatment of the frozen levels is missing. In the limit the moduli up to Q^a (a < 1) need more entropy than they have, so all but those within a bounded factor of x are frozen and the top moduli must strike all the rows these leave, 0.7413·π(Q)/ln x, from classes that hold O(1) of them: D(n) ≤ (e^γ/(2C₂) + o(1))·r ln² r/ln ln r, and greedy on the top reaches the same order. That part is a heuristic of one day. The consultant's first check confirmed it and the research session recorded that at about 11:20 UTC; the confirmation was withdrawn at about 11:30 UTC: the Lean session's referee read shows that the small moduli can be set to leave far fewer rows than random classes (box ‘A structured prefix beats random classes’), so the bound with 1/ln ln r is not derived. The turn of the table is the statement about typical covers. A direct test of the freezing (the sampled complete covers are counted setting by setting): at 167 moduli the 41 smallest moduli (up to 181), which have 165 nats of classes to choose from, occur in 6 different settings among 1.1 million sampled complete covers at Q = 40,111 (1.1 nats of entropy, where the recursion as it was needs −42 and the constrained one has 0.0), in 21 settings among 1.4 million at Q = 38,000 (2.6 nats), and in 40,481 settings at Q = 25,000, where the constraint does not yet bind. The freezing sets in where the constraint starts to bind and reaches as far up the moduli as the constrained recursion says (16 settings of the first 61 moduli at 40,111, thousands of the first 90); beyond the frozen part the measured entropy grows more slowly than the recursion's, and among the first dozen moduli the recursion spreads the entropy wrongly. One start in one family. A cross-check of the consultant's measurement, from the constrained solution at the end of complete covers (research session, 11:56 UTC): the rows alive after the moduli up to x/ln x, as a share of what random classes leave on the same moduli, are 0.741 at x = 9,973 and 0.772 at x = 1,999, against 0.72 to 0.74 for greedy classes on real primes, and not the 0.36 that the entropy cap would have allowed. In the solution the frozen moduli do what greedy does (a frozen level takes its largest class); the difference between its end (1.0·x ln² x) and greedy's (0.71) is made above x/ln x, by the moduli from 0.1x to 0.4x (still frozen, weights near 1) and by the top half, where the alive rows fall from 0.29 of random at x/2 to nothing. Whether real covers can do that at this size cannot be checked at 1,228 moduli; at 89 moduli the recursion with the Lean session's exact dispersions puts the end 5% too far, which the research session reads as the size of the overstatement.

nodes.title: A capacity bound for the top primes: each strikes about ln x/ln ln x rows (for covers whose small moduli act like random classes)
nodes.gist: The research session withdrew its limit 1.1275 on 25 Nov, putting order r ln² r/ln ln r in its place, and asked for an attack on that argument; this is the consultant's check. Split the moduli into small ones (up to x/ω) and top ones. If the small ones leave what random classes leave, 2C₂e^(−γ)·π(Q)/ln x rows, a complete cover needs the largest classes of the top primes to add up to that; with less than one alive row per class near x the largest class holds only ln x/(ln ln x − 1) rows, so such covers end at about 1.349·x ln² x/(ln ln x − 1). The premise fails for structured small moduli (next box), so this is not a bound on D(x), and the verdict that D/(x ln² x) tends to 0 was withdrawn the same day.
nodes.detail: Tested on real primes, and these tests stand. Greedy covers reach D/(x ln² x) = 0.55 (x = 151), 0.66 (2,000), 0.72 (2·10⁴ to 10⁵). Greedy classes on the small moduli leave 0.72 to 0.74 of the alive rows a random choice leaves, flat from x = 300 to 10⁵ (the research session's constrained recursion has 0.74 at the same point, x = 9,973, and 0.77 at x = 1,999). At x = 2·10⁴ the largest top classes found add up to 7,361 against 8,041 for Poisson class sizes. Fitted to these two factors the model puts the maximum of D/(x ln² x) for greedy covers at x = 10⁵ to 10⁶ (0.73) and gives 0.69 at 10⁹ and 0.52 at 10³⁰ (shape, not value). What was wrong: the bulk was taken to have a Gaussian lower tail, so that the entropy of the small moduli allows only a saving of about 2/√ln x. A block of moduli (z, x/4] all given the class of one common integer near Q has entropy about ln x nats and leaves 0.93, 0.86, 0.72 and 0.57 of the rows a random choice leaves at x = 10⁴, 10⁵, 10⁶ and 3.75·10⁶, with no limit to the saving (the Lean session's table: 0.07 at ln x = 1000). The structured prefix the check tried (all classes 1) was the wrong family. Not proved, for typical covers: Poisson class sizes of the alive primes in progressions out to class size ln x/ln ln x.

nodes.title: Seven mechanisms outside the closure grammar, scored on the exact miniature
nodes.gist: The lead asked for at least five mechanisms not in the grammar L of the closure theorem, each scored as nats gained against cover first on the miniature, negative results included. Seven were scored on three miniatures (N below 10⁹ and below 2·10⁹ at Q = 1,000, N below 10⁹ at Q = 900), each tested out of sample. Anything computed from the residues mod 3 to 23 is worth at most about 0.1 nats; the size of N 0.1 to 0.3 (about 0.1 at 200 digits); neighbours of found successes 0.02; a coherent block, N/2 prime and the neighbourhood of perfect squares nothing or less. One reaches 1.4 nats when verification is free and does not survive.

nodes.title: Neighbours of near-successes: +1.45 nats on the miniature, +0.035 at the campaign's cover
nodes.gist: Take cover-first members with at most five prime rows and score their neighbours N + s, only for shifts that share many rows with N and put none of the seed's prime rows on a prime row of N + s: the shared rows are then composite for free. On the miniature (rows left ≤ 30) 1.7 million neighbour scans find 80 new distinct successes beside the stream's 47, for 4.31 million units against 18.35 million for cover first at 127 successes: +1.45 nats. Out of sample +0.9 to +1.56 (N below 2·10⁹) and +0.7 to +1.36 (Q = 900); below a nat at 30 successes or fewer.
nodes.detail: By the identity the research session supplied, the neighbours of a stream member hold at most the success mass of all its neighbours: on the miniature the sum over 126 shifts of exp(−p·(rows(N + s) − rows(N))) is 5.6, 7.7, 10.5 and 14.0 times the member's own mass (stream prefixes 28 to 31), against 0.036 at the campaign's cover (89 moduli, 1,248 rows alive at Q = 170,000, p = 0.02398, computed by FFT over every even shift: the research session, commit 623e94c, not recomputed here). So the ceiling at 200 digits is +0.035 nats if rejecting neighbours were free and about +0.00005 for the part worth testing. The quantity that decides it is p times the number of rows a neighbour inherits: about 4 on the miniature, 11 to 12 at the campaign's size. With verification priced in modexps (a seed with at most J prime rows costs (J + 1)/0.5 tests per stream member against 2.2 for rejection) the 15 cells run give −0.82 to +0.23. nodes.title: Where the missing 5.4 nats are not: the arithmetic of the rows, the prime-gap toolbox, the covering theorems
nodes.gist: The lead asked where the 5.4 nats between the budget and g ≥ 200,000 could come from. Seven candidates in the arithmetic of the rows were given numbers: an algebraic form N = a² + c nets −6.6 nats, second-order Hardy–Littlewood −0.03, the size of N inside the decade at most 0.08, rows as extra moduli 0.24 nats for 6.3 nats of entropy, annealing the cover 1,576 → 1,524 rows (the campaign has 1,502), selection inside a class vector 1.9 to 3.4 nats collectable (6.6 at an infinite sieve budget), and a floor of 12.5 to 41.7 modular exponentiations to reach the first prime. The prime-gap record toolbox (Troisi's combined sieve) lowers no exponent, and the covering theorems of Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao and Freiberg are vacuous at x = 463.
nodes.detail: Setting: Q = 200,000, the 89 odd moduli 3 to 463, 1,502 rows alive, p = 0.02398, exponent 36.46 nats. An algebraic form: F(c) = primes of the form c + b² below Q is at most 155 (mean 20); after the cover 15 are alive, worth 0.36 nats, and CRT can then pin only the primes up to 229 (49 moduli instead of 89), +238 rows. Second order: measured on 1,576 alive rows with the exact pair factor over all 1.24 million pairs: the two pieces are −0.221 and +0.190 and cancel (the pair factor averages to 1 over differences). Selection: survivors after a sieve to B are binomial (mean 548, sd 19 at 2·10⁷); verifying only the best fraction gives 2.9, 2.6, 1.9 nats at sieve costs 0.003, 0.01, 0.1 modexps per member (B = 10⁶). The covering theorems: the smallness hypothesis of Corollary 4 needs ln x ≥ 10⁵ against 6.1 at x = 463, and the guaranteed gap is 1.8 integers where greedy covers 1 to 1,321. Later check (Opus session, `two_stage/b_answer.md`): the fleet's constant of 1.5 tests per unit of hit mass already contains a hard cut on the survivors, within 0.1 to 0.2 nat of its optimum, so the selection row is not additional.

nodes.title: The lattice claim attacked and not broken: no Coppersmith-type decoder gets past 0.36 of the agreement it needs
nodes.gist: The research session's claim that lattice decoding cannot reach the aligned members of a window was attacked on a cover of my own (1,524 rows) with every variant I could find: the typical member has 0.21 of the agreement a Howgrave-Graham/Coppersmith decoder needs and the best member of a whole simulated window (2·10⁷ members, +5.41 sd) 0.25; hard lists with their true sizes 0.25 and 0.30; soft weights, the strongest variant, have a closed form (ratio² ≤ ln(1 + n/x)/ln K = 0.086, so at most 0.294 typical and about 0.36 best); products of shifted copies fall (0.200 to 0.116), subsets of rows grow with their size. The claim stands.
nodes.detail: To reach 1 the decoder would need a window of at most 2.1 nats (about 8 members) where the cover leaves 16.9; pinning first reaches 1 only at ln K′ = 0.7. Cost even where the bound holds: dimension at least 1,524 with entries of at least 5,000 bits, at least 2.7·10¹⁶ bit-operations for one decoding against 3·10¹⁰ marks to sieve the whole window. The member is not hidden: its agreement pattern carries about 136 nats against ln K = 16.9, so it is identified; the obstruction is computational. Wording agreed with the research session: 'no Coppersmith-type decoder reaches the aligned members', not 'no lattice method'. The same note reproduces the isolated-number accounting; its loss of 1.2 to 1.6 nats was revised in the bottom-up round to 1.9 to 3.4 nats once the per-number sieve is counted in cycles.

nodes.title: The bottom-up round: the accounting of the 460 nats, a model that reproduces the 69 published records, and no new source of information
nodes.gist: Asked to discover new mathematics or build from the bottom up, the helper session found nothing that lowers the 36.46 nats and put numbers on why. The one entropy is ln 10²⁰⁰ = 460.5 nats: even N alone leaves an exponent of 78.3, avoiding the small primes 52.2 (1.7 nats), optimised classes 36.46 (443 nats, 0.036 nats per nat), and 16.9 nats remain as the window. A pin beyond 463 pays 0.035 nats per nat at 467 and 0.002 at 200,003. The good members of a simulated window have no additive structure beyond shared pins (energy 1.0000). The success model reproduces the 69 published records of the least Goldbach summand with an excess of +0.06 ± 0.34 nats for N ≥ 8·10¹³, where the exponent is 30 to 40 nats.
nodes.detail: Rates: the cover is a Gaussian-tail selection with 0.58 nats per sd (sd 24.0 rows over random covers) and a random-energy optimum of 17.3 nats against the 15.8 taken; the window has 1.33 nats per sd. Supply of covers: e^21 covers lie within 8 rows of the best (checked), against e^19.7 needed, a cost of 0.12 to 0.19 nats. Research's three literature points: Bernstein's batch smooth part costs 2,900 to 8,700 Fermat tests per member in wall-clock (the 2 to 5 of bit-operation counting is off by a factor of about 750), per-number root lookups 85 to 530; no integer analogue of the Joux/Swan relations (no group acts on a sparse row set); the number field sieve's root sieve is a scan. Corrections: a lone ideal N costs 1.9 to 3.4 nats (the per-N sieve to 10⁶ is 1.2 to 7 tests in cycles), and the window sieve costs 0.075 to 0.13 tests per member. Literature on the bare problem: nothing below the Johnson-type threshold for random lists; hardness is worst-case or conditional; the same regime is the Polynomial Reconstruction assumption. A grammar-closing heuristic: Hypothesis H and Chowla/Sarnak allow exactly pins and reducible forms as systematic relations.
